summary: Defines standard terminology and a taxonomy for web replication and caching, describing the pieces and protocols in use at the time. It is informational.

eli5.summary: People use the same words for different things, so this gives everyone one set of names for the helpers that copy and store websites to make them load faster.

questions: what is web replication and caching taxonomy
what is a surrogate in web caching
what is the difference between a proxy and a reverse proxy
subtitle: A shared vocabulary and map of the protocols behind web caches, proxies and replicated servers.

tldr.problem: As the web grew, replication and caching became core infrastructure, but people used the same words for different things and the protocols involved were scattered across many documents.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines terms, describes the relationships among clients, replicas, proxies and network elements, and then catalogs the protocols for each relationship with a description, security notes and deployment notes.
tldr.outcome: It gives a common reference point and is intended to help build a standard architecture for webs that include both replicas and caches.

today: RFC 3040 is an Informational memo and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It describes protocols as deployed in January 2001, and several it cites were still work in progress at that time.

sections.title: Why a Taxonomy
sections.content:
Since its introduction in 1990, the Web grew from a simple client-server model into a complex distributed architecture, largely because of scaling problems. Two core components used to meet that growth are replication and caching, and the two often need to coexist.

This memo sets out standard terminology and a taxonomy of the infrastructure deployed at the time. Some protocols it covers are specified only by white papers or work in progress, and are included to show that they exist or are in experimental use. Known problems with caching proxies are left to a separate document, "Known HTTP Proxy/Caching Problems".
sections.eli5: Many people were building web helpers and calling the same thing by different names. This memo gives them a shared list.

sections.title: Terminology
sections.content:
Base terms such as client, server, proxy, cache, gateway and tunnel are taken from RFC 2616. A caching proxy is a proxy with a cache. A surrogate is a gateway working on behalf of one or more origin servers, usually answering from an internal cache; devices called reverse proxies and server accelerators are more properly surrogates.

Replication terms include master origin server and replica origin server. Topological terms include cache array, a cluster of caching proxies acting as one service and partitioning the resource name space, and caching mesh, a loosely coupled set of cooperating proxies sharing cacheable content.

The memo also takes a position on naming. In RFC 2616, a "transparent proxy" is one that does not modify requests or responses beyond what authentication needs. The caching community used the same phrase for proxies needing no client configuration, so the memo introduces interception proxy for proxies that receive traffic redirected by a network element.
sections.eli5: The memo gives each helper one clear name, and gives a new name to the one that had been confusing everyone.

sections.title: Relationships Between Components
sections.content:
The memo describes the relationships in a distributed system. A client may talk to replica origin servers and a master origin server, and replicas talk to each other. A client may use zero or more local proxies, or zero or more surrogates that it treats as if they were origin servers.

Proxies relate to each other as loosely coupled meshes, with peers and parents, or as tightly coupled arrays. In its example mesh, a peer may only be used when it already holds the resource, while a parent is the local proxy's choice. A network element doing traffic interception may redirect client requests to a proxy in an array, either in-line or out-of-path.
sections.eli5: Some helpers keep copies of websites, some pass requests along, and some work in teams. The memo draws who talks to whom.

sections.title: Protocols by Relationship
sections.content:
Each protocol entry gives a best known reference, a description, security notes, deployment notes and a submitter. They are grouped by relationship:

  • Replica selection: navigation hyperlinks, HTTP redirection (such as 302 and 307), and DNS redirection, where a DNS server sorts addresses from most to least optimal replica.
  • Inter-replica: batch driven, demand driven and synchronized replication.
  • User agent to proxy: manual configuration, Proxy Auto Configuration (PAC), CARP v1.0 and WPAD, whose only goal is to locate the PAC URL.
  • Inter-proxy: ICP, HTCP, Cache Digest and cache pre-filling for loosely coupled caches, and CARP for tightly coupled ones.
  • Network element: WCCP, NECP and SOCKS.

For example, ICP uses UDP to ask other proxies whether they hold a resource (RFC 2186), while HTCP requests include HTTP header material that ICP lacks (RFC 2756). Cache Digests instead fetch a summary of a peer's cache contents so no exchange is needed per request.
sections.eli5: For every kind of helper-to-helper chat there is a listed way to do it, with notes on how safe it is and who uses it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo does not describe recommended practice in detail, and points to each protocol's own documentation and to RFC 2616 for HTTP proxy security. It names several concerns: proxies are men-in-the-middle, clients must trust a caching proxy to act for the origin server, and IP-number authentication is problematic behind a proxy.

On privacy, a proxy sees every request from its users, so its logs are more sensitive than a web server log. Redirection is open to denial of service at the redirect point, and the memo says it has been argued that an interception proxy is itself a denial of service attack because it destroys end-to-end behavior without the user's knowledge. It also notes that a caching proxy is by definition a replay attack, and that end-to-end encryption frequently makes resources uncacheable. Legal questions about transient copies are noted but not covered.
sections.eli5: A helper in the middle sees everything that passes through, so you have to trust it and keep its notes private.
